quote: the midpoint of my life's journey
note: The Bible gives a life as seventy years (Psalm 90), so Dante is 35. Born in 1265, he sets the journey at Easter 1300. His Italian says "our life", not "my life": from the first line, his journey stands for everyone's.
Usually read as sin and spiritual confusion, a life gone astray. Dante never says what his own straying was. In Purgatorio 30–31, Beatrice reproaches him for turning to other things after her death.
Sleep as the dulling of the soul. Sin creeps up unnoticed, so Dante can't say when he left the true way.

The hill is the happy, virtuous life Dante hopes to climb to, and its sunlit summit a first glimpse of God's grace. He will learn that he can't climb it directly: the way up leads first down through Hell.

quote: that star which guides all travelers true
note: The sun. In the earth-centered astronomy Dante used, the sun was one of the planets circling the earth. It guides travelers on the road, and stands for God's light guiding the soul.
Medieval medicine placed a hollow in the heart where the blood gathered, and fear was felt there. Dante makes it a lake, still troubled after the night.

quote: Like a man who, gasping for breath
note: The first of the poem's many extended similes: a shipwrecked man on the beach, turning back to stare at the sea that nearly drowned him. The forest was Dante's sea.

quote: no living person has ever escaped
note: The way of sin leads to death, of the soul as well as the body. Dante is the exception, and the poem is the story of how.

quote: always placing my weight on the lower foot
note: A famously puzzling line. Literally, a climber's back foot is the lower one. Many readers take it as a limp: the soul's "firm foot", its will, still drags behind as it tries to climb toward virtue.

context: Its bright spotted coat, the spring morning and the rising sun give Dante hope that he can get past it.

quote: the sun was rising with those same stars
note: The sun is in the constellation Aries, where medieval tradition said it stood when God created the world in spring. The journey starts on a morning like the first morning of creation.
Spring, the week of Easter.

context: The beast Dante can't get past. Virgil will say she lets no one by, and grows hungrier the more she eats.

note: Dante describes darkness as silence, mixing the senses: he is being driven back down to the forest, where no light reaches.

The Italian can mean faint or dim as well as hoarse. Read literally, it is a shade who hasn't spoken in centuries. Read as allegory, it is reason, so long ignored by Dante that its voice has grown weak.
An anachronism: the Lombards, who gave the region its name, arrived in Italy six centuries after Virgil. Dante uses the name of his own day.

context: Virgil was born in 70 BC, years before Caesar came to power. "Late" is usually read as too late: Virgil was still young when Caesar was killed, and never wrote under him.

note: The gods of Rome, which Virgil, now in the afterlife, knows to have been false.

context: Virgil doesn't name his hero, only his father, as the Aeneid often does. "Righteous" is Virgil's own word for him there.

note: Troy, called proud Ilium in the Aeneid. The Greeks burned it after ten years of war.
The sunlit hill of the opening lines.

context: Dante recognizes him with awe. The poet he learned his craft from will be his guide.

note: The high style of Dante's earlier love poems, which he says he learned from Virgil's book.

A riddle. It may mean between the towns of Feltre and Montefeltro, a region that would point to Cangrande della Scala of Verona. Or it may mean "between felt and felt": felt was a humble cloth, so a humble birth.
A phrase from the Aeneid, where Aeneas's sailors first sight Italy low on the horizon. Humble there means low-lying.

Fallen of the Aeneid's war in Italy. Nisus and Euryalus were young Trojan friends who died together on a night raid. Turnus was the Italian prince Aeneas killed in the poem's last lines. Dante mixes the dead of both sides, as if all died for the same Italy.

quote: from where envy first released her
note: The devil's envy, which brought death into the world, in the Book of Wisdom (2:24).

context: Virgil sketches the whole journey in three steps: Hell first, then Purgatory, then Heaven with another guide.

note: The damned long for a death that would end their existence, and with it their pain. Revelation calls damnation itself the second death (20:14).

context: The souls in Purgatory suffer in fire, but gladly, because they know they will reach Heaven.
Beatrice, not yet named. She will take Virgil's place as guide at the top of Purgatory.

note: God, described in the language of empire that Virgil, a Roman, would know. "Everywhere he governs, but there he reigns": God rules all things, but his throne is in Heaven.

quote: because I rebelled against his law
note: Virgil was no rebel. He lived before Christ and never knew God, and in Dante's theology that alone shuts him out of Heaven. Inferno 4 shows where he spends eternity.
Probably the gate of Purgatory, kept by an angel who holds Saint Peter's keys (Purgatorio 9). Some read it as the gate of Heaven itself.
